extracted.intended_audience: commanding officers, judge advocates, military legal practitioners, and officers responsible for courts-martial and discipline
extracted.subtask_description: A practical/legal digest of rules governing military discipline, preparation and preferral of charges, courts-martial constitution and procedure, evidence, findings and sentences, records, and review of court-martial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to discharge enlisted men
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth article of war vests in the commanding officer of a department specific authority to discharge enlisted men; department commanders have incident power to order discharge of undesirable soldiers in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There can be no doubt as to the authority of the commanding general of the department to order discharge; however some discharges (e.g., on account of disability) may be reserved to War Department action. Examples: department commander ordered discharge without honor of clearly undesirable soldiers; commanding officer, district of North Alaska could not be given authority to discharge on surgeon's certificate of disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of nature of discharge in disability cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanding officer/commanding general may determine from medical officer's report the nature of the discharge in disability cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disability was contracted in the line of duty an honorable discharge issues. If the disability is shown to be due to the vicious habits of the soldier, an honorable discharge cannot issue and separation will be a discharge without honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on who may impose certain discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial cannot impose either an honorable discharge or a discharge without honor, nor can a dishonorable discharge be imposed except by sentence of court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discharges of various kinds have statutory/procedural limits as to who may impose them; only court-martial sentence may impose dishonorable discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to reenlist is not basis for discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who honestly changes his mind and declines to reenlist cannot have that change of intention used as a basis for granting him a discharge without honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to grant commanding general authority to issue discharges without honor in such cases was denied; an honest change of intention does not taint character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of honorable (and without-honor) discharge on prior enlistment offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: An honorable discharge releases from the particular contract and term of enlistment to which it relates, and does not relieve the soldier from the consequences of a desertion committed during a prior enlistment; similarly held with respect to a discharge without honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discharges release the soldier from amenability for offenses charged against him within the particular term to which they relate, including desertion, except as provided in the sixtieth article of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of dishonorable discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonorable discharge is a discharge from the military service as a punishment — a complete expulsion from the Army — and covers all unexpired enlistments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A soldier thus dishonorably discharged cannot be made amenable for a desertion or other military offense committed under a prior enlistment except as provided in the sixtieth article of war; a subsequent enlistment after such dishonorable discharge does not revive amenability for such offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against summary discharge for long-serving NCOs
rubrics_metrics.description: A noncommissioned officer of a number of years' standing is entitled to consideration and no man should be summarily discharged for an actual concrete offense without being given ample opportunity to present a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation against summarily discharging long-serving NCOs absent opportunity to justify their acts (case cited: post commissary sergeant charged with irregularities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest — permissible force and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: As much force as is necessary may be used in arrest, but a private house cannot be entered (public parts of a public house excepted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest rules specify permissible force, and limitations on entering dwellings; see further subrules re: status and procedural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest status and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrest does not involve irons; may be inconsistent with duty; an officer in arrest can prefer charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual lists status implications of arrest and procedural interactions with charges and trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bail cannot be accepted for arrests
rubrics_metrics.description: Bail cannot be accepted when a person is placed in arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest rules make clear that bail is not an available procedural device in this status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' arrest — who may place and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are placed in arrest by the commanding officer only; arrest is not a demandable right; there are rules on the manner of placing in arrest and limits of arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details include who may effect arrest, appropriate procedures, and that arrest is discretionary, not a right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest of enlisted men — by whom and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlisted men may be arrested by noncommissioned officers, but cannot be punished summarily and tried for the same offense; paroled by civil courts can be arrested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies NCO authority and prohibition on double summary punishment and trial for same offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges — structure and essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation of charges consists of two parts; each charge may have several specifications; each specification must be appropriate to its charge; reference to a writing should quote the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charges must be prepared with definite terms, under the proper article of war, and essentials set out; the drafting rules emphasize clarity and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges — drafting prohibitions and drafting particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not plead evidence, do not plead secondary evidence, do not plead minor included offense, and do not plead alternatively; use definite terms, allege time and place appropriately (e.g., 'on or about', 'at or near'), and describe persons without using first-person pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time should be reasonably exact (options like 'from — to —', 'between — and —' in omissions); charges may recite article numbers and tailor allegations to statutory requirements; numerous article-specific drafting notes (20th, 21st, 58th, 60th, 61st articles) are supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signing and preferring charges — timing and signatory rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges must be signed (rules on by whom), may be preferred 'at once after commission of offense', and there are rules on accumulation of charges and forwarding by the commanding officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual addresses who signs when the Judge Advocate General prepares charges, and notes that commanding officers when forwarding charges are not required to state character of accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment, withdrawal, and disposition of charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges may be amended before trial and may be withdrawn; there are rules for disposition of original charges after arraignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural controls on changing the charges ensure fairness and proper notice to the accused; pleas in abatement and amendment mechanisms are described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convening authority — constitution and duties of court
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations as to constitution of court are mandatory; convening authority appoints members, judge advocate, and must consider availability, bias, and rank; authority over court exists but some delegations are forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convening authority must show authority in convening order, may consolidate charges, may direct nolle prosequi, may afford accused explanation, and cannot routinely delegate appointment as a staff duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Advocate — powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge advocate is separate for each court; has authority to alter charges, employ a reporter, subpoena witnesses (including by deposition), certify witness locating expenses, employ expert witnesses (e.g., insanity), issue process, prepare and authenticate the record, administer oaths, and advise the court and the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge advocate has no authority over the accused; duties include preparing the record, authenticating it, and executing orders of the court; counsel to assist judge advocate only in important/complicated cases; judge advocate's details and conflicts of interest are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of the accused
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused cannot be compelled to incriminate himself; rights of the accused are independent of his rank; trial is not a 'right' in some contexts; defense should be afforded minimum restraint to prevent embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel is not an automatic right; accused may have interviews with counsel, may employ civil counsel at his own expense, and may make statements (if written, must be signed); accused's admissions bind him and he should be allowed freedom of expression in statement; failure to note variance at arraignment constitutes waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arraignment and plea rules
rubrics_metrics.description: At arraignment, if accused declines to plead, plea 'not guilty' is entered; a guilty plea may allow the accused to call for evidence but evidence is not to be received by plea alone; changing a plea is governed by rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One act with several charges, changing plea procedures, and interaction between plea and evidence (e.g., statement made with plea) are governed; plea of guilty does not bar court from receiving certain evidence in limited circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special pleas, motions, and trial suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Special pleas (plea in bar such as pardon, pleas in abatement) and motions (to strike out) are recognized; trial may be suspended when accused develops insanity; closed sessions and limitations on judge-advocate/exclusions are specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules address when closed sessions may occur, when judge-advocate may be excluded, and limits on motions and pleas; polling, voting, and adjournment rules (majority required) are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness competence and summoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on competent witnesses (e.g., deserter, members, judge advocate, reviewing authority) and incompetent witnesses (e.g., wife of accused in certain cases, insane persons, children in certain offenses); accused is entitled to summoning of material witnesses but cannot demand certain important witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service of summons can be by military or civil person and cannot be hired; depositions allowed under the ninety-first article; fees, expert witnesses, and procedures for witnesses in foreign territory are addressed; writ of attachment when summons not obeyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of evidence are the same as in United States criminal courts; presumption that officer performs duty; burden of proof rules (e.g., desertion cases); privileged communications; confessions must be free and voluntary and cannot be used until corpus delicti is proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility, weight of evidence (does not depend on number of witnesses), documentary evidence hierarchy (official records high-class evidence; compiled statements not admitted), affidavits not admitted, and special rules on repeating prior hearing evidence (must be given de novo) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary evidence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Official records made pursuant to special objects for which they are kept are high-class evidence; copies of War Department orders, morning reports, pay accounts, descriptive lists, and court-martial records have specific admissibility rules; private writings under military control require proof of handwriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compiled statements are not admitted; affidavits are not admitted; telegrams and private writings not under military control require additional proof; distinctions are made between documents within War Department control and those outside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings — support and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding on a charge must be supported by a finding on the specification; separate finding required on each charge and specification; court cannot substitute a finding of an offense other than the one charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One charge-one specification relationships, lesser included offense rules (e.g., AWOL instead of desertion), exceptions and permitted substitutions (name, rank, time) are explained; special article-specific proof requirements (21st, 38th, etc.) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing — admissibility and measurement of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of previous convictions may be admitted to determine the measure of punishment; in discretionary cases court may impose any punishment sanctioned by customs of service; maximum punishment orders guide measure and kind of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convening authority cannot order a court to adopt a particular form of sentence; punishment should be measured by the gravity of the military offense. Rules for adoption of sentence (each member proposes and votes), and types of punishment (reprimand, forfeiture, loss of rank, confinement) and their formal requirements (e.g., forfeiture must state exact amount) are detailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confinement and forfeiture rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences of confinement should state 'at such place as the reviewing authority may designate'; confinement may extend beyond term of service; forfeiture must clearly state the penalty and exact amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may consider time already spent in confinement; court cannot sentence man to forfeit private money; fines to reimburse Government for certain costs are impermissible; limits on unusual punishments and formalities for loss of rank are set out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper sentences include ordering the accused to perform duty, to remain in service, or to deposit pay with the paymaster (as a sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples of improper sentences are provided to guide courts away from punitive acts that are not lawful sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to clemency and remarks by court
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations to clemency are not part of the record; there may be more than one recommendation, members should state specific ground for recommendation, and such recommendations cannot be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should clearly state grounds for clemency recommendations; remarks by court and animadversion upon witnesses are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record keeping requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of courts-martial must be a full recital of the details of trial and include convening order, organization, all meetings, testimony, and a separate record for each case; death sentence record must state two-thirds vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records must set proceedings in proper order; revisions and reconvenings have strict rules (e.g., five members for reconvened court, no new testimony in certain revisions); indorsement by judge advocate does not amend record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing authority — scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewing authority (often the original convening authority) cannot be restrained by superior authority, cannot delegate functions, and the sentence is inchoate until acted on by the reviewing authority; the reviewing authority may return the record for specified reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for returning include materially erroneous record, improper findings, errors in time alleged, or failure to afford rights (denying witness, member absent for substantial part, member acted as judge advocate, etc.). Presumption that proceedings are regular applies; irregularities not fatal are enumerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction of court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction is criminal, not civil; it is not territorial; there is no presumption in favor of jurisdiction; jurisdiction attaches when person is placed in arrest or charges served; jurisdiction over civilians by military courts is generally unconstitutional except limited exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double jeopardy rules and the conditions under which jurisdiction is retained or lost (e.g., with separation from service) are explained; special notes on civilians, general prisoners, and changes in status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convening order formal requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The convening order must show that the convening officer had authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal requirement for the validity of a court-martial; absence of authority in the convening order can be grounds for challenge.
